title: Supplement: Estimation Theory

blocks.x: This supplementary chapter proves what Chapter 1 states without proof:
why the sample mean is the MVUE for a normal mean;
how much precision is possible at all (the Cram'er–Rao bound);
why the maximum likelihood estimator is asymptotically optimal;
what it means for a statistic to carry all the information about a parameter (sufficiency).
It is for readers who want the mathematics behind Chapter 1. The textbook’s problems do not need it.
Let $X$ have density (or mass function) $f(x;\theta)$ with a scalar parameter $\theta$. Assume the usual regularity conditions:
the support of $f$ does not depend on $\theta$;
$f$ is twice differentiable in $\theta$;
differentiation and integration can be interchanged.
The score is $U(\theta)=\dfrac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\ln f(X;\theta)$.
The Fisher information of one observation is $\Fish(\theta)=\Var\big(U(\theta)\big)$.
For a random sample of size $n$ the information is $n\Fish(\theta)$.
Under regularity, $\Exp[U(\theta)]=0$ and
\Fish(\theta)=\Exp\Big[\Big(\frac{\partial\ln f}{\partial\theta}\Big)^2\Big]=-\Exp\Big[\frac{\partial^2\ln f}{\partial\theta^2}\Big].
Since $\int f(x;\theta)\,dx=1$, differentiating gives $0=\int\partial_\theta f\,dx=\int(\partial_\theta\ln f)f\,dx=\Exp[U]$.
Differentiate $\int(\partial_\theta\ln f)f\,dx=0$ once more:
0=\int(\partial_\theta^2\ln f)f\,dx+\int(\partial_\theta\ln f)\partial_\theta f\,dx=\Exp[\partial_\theta^2\ln f]+\Exp[U^2].
Since $\Exp[U]=0$, $\Var[U]=\Exp[U^2]=-\Exp[\partial_\theta^2\ln f]$.
The second form says: information is the expected curvature of the log-likelihood. A sharply peaked likelihood pins down $\theta$ precisely.
Bernoulli$(p)$: $\ln f=x\ln p+(1-x)\ln(1-p)$ and $\partial^2\ln f/\partial p^2=-x/p^2-(1-x)/(1-p)^2$. So $\Fish(p)=1/p+1/(1-p)=\dfrac1{p(1-p)}$.
Poisson$(\lambda)$: $\ln f=x\ln\lambda-\lambda-\ln x!$. $\Fish(\lambda)=\Exp[X]/\lambda^2=1/\lambda$.
Exponential with rate $\lambda$: $\ln f=\ln\lambda-\lambda x$. $\Fish(\lambda)=1/\lambda^2$.
$\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2)$: with $\sigma^2$ known, $\Fish(\mu)=1/\sigma^2$. With $\mu$ known, $\Fish(\sigma^2)=1/(2\sigma^4)$.
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be a random sample and $\hat\Theta$ an unbiased estimator of $\theta$. Under regularity,
\Var(\hat\Theta)\ \ge\ \frac1{n\Fish(\theta)}.
More generally, if $\Exp[\hat\Theta]=\theta+b(\theta)$, then $\Var(\hat\Theta)\ge[1+b'(\theta)]^2/(n\Fish(\theta))$.
Let $U_n=\sum_i\partial_\theta\ln f(X_i;\theta)$ be the score of the whole sample. Then $\Exp[U_n]=0$ and $\Var[U_n]=n\Fish(\theta)$.
For unbiased $\hat\Theta$, $\theta=\Exp[\hat\Theta]=\int\hat\theta(\mathbf{x})f(\mathbf{x};\theta)\,d\mathbf{x}$. Differentiate in $\theta$:
1=\int\hat\theta\,\partial_\theta f\,d\mathbf{x}=\Exp[\hat\Theta U_n]=\Cov(\hat\Theta,U_n),
using $\Exp[U_n]=0$. By Cauchy–Schwarz for covariances,
1=\Cov(\hat\Theta,U_n)^2\le\Var(\hat\Theta)\Var(U_n)=\Var(\hat\Theta)\,n\Fish(\theta).
An unbiased estimator whose variance equals the Cram'er–Rao bound is efficient. The efficiency of an unbiased estimator is the bound divided by its variance. It is at most $1$.

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: $\bar{X}$ is the MVUE for a normal mean

blocks.x: For $X_i\sim\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma^2$ known, $\bar{X}$ is efficient: $\Var[\bar{X}]=\sigma^2/n=1/(n\Fish(\mu))$. Hence $\bar{X}$ is the MVUE of $\mu$ (Theorem 1.9 of Chapter 1).
Bernoulli sample: $\Var[\hat{P}]=p(1-p)/n=1/(n\Fish(p))$. The sample proportion is efficient.
$\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2)$: $\Var[S^2]=2\sigma^4/(n-1)$, while the bound for unbiased estimators of $\sigma^2$ is $2\sigma^4/n$. So $S^2$ is not efficient, but its efficiency $(n-1)/n\to1$.

blocks.name: Common pitfall
blocks.title: when the bound does not apply

blocks.x: The regularity conditions fail when the support depends on the parameter.

For the uniform distribution on $(0,\theta)$, the unbiased estimator $\frac{n+1}n\max X_i$ has variance $\theta^2/(n(n+2))$, of order $1/n^2$. That is smaller than the order-$1/n$ value the formal Cram'er–Rao expression would give. There is no contradiction: the bound is not valid for this family.

sections.title: Asymptotic properties of the maximum likelihood estimator

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: Asymptotic normality and efficiency of the MLE

blocks.x: Under regularity, the MLE $\hat\Theta_n$ from $n$ i.i.d. observations is consistent, and
\sqrt n\big(\hat\Theta_n-\theta\big)\xrightarrow{d}\Normal\Big(0,\frac1{\Fish(\theta)}\Big).
So for large $n$, $\hat\Theta_n\approx\Normal\big(\theta,\ 1/(n\Fish(\theta))\big)$. The MLE reaches the Cram'er–Rao bound asymptotically.
Let $\ell(\theta)=\sum\ln f(X_i;\theta)$. Expand the likelihood equation $\ell'(\hat\theta)=0$ about the true $\theta$:
0=\ell'(\theta)+(\hat\theta-\theta)\ell''(\tilde\theta)\quad\text{for some }\tilde\theta\text{ between }\hat\theta\text{ and }\theta.
Hence
\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta)=\frac{n^{-1/2}\ell'(\theta)}{-n^{-1}\ell''(\tilde\theta)}.
The numerator is $n^{-1/2}$ times a sum of i.i.d. scores with mean $0$ and variance $\Fish(\theta)$. By the CLT it tends to $\Normal(0,\Fish(\theta))$.
The denominator tends in probability to $-\Exp[\partial^2\ln f]=\Fish(\theta)$, by the law of large numbers. (Consistency lets us replace $\tilde\theta$ by $\theta$.)
By Slutsky’s theorem the ratio tends to $\Normal(0,\Fish(\theta)/\Fish(\theta)^2)=\Normal(0,1/\Fish(\theta))$.
Approximate two-sided $100(1-\alpha)\%$ interval: $\hat\theta\pm z_{\alpha/2}/\sqrt{n\Fish(\hat\theta)}$.
One-sided $100(1-\alpha)\%$ bounds use $z_\alpha$ and one limit: $\theta\le\hat\theta+z_\alpha/\sqrt{n\Fish(\hat\theta)}$, or $\hat\theta-z_\alpha/\sqrt{n\Fish(\hat\theta)}\le\theta$.
To test $H_0:\theta=\theta_0$, use $Z=(\hat\theta-\theta_0)\sqrt{n\Fish(\theta_0)}$ (or $\hat\theta$ in place of $\theta_0$ inside $\Fish$). It is approximately $\Normal(0,1)$ under $H_0$.
$n=200$ exponential observations with $\bar{x}=4$.
$\hat\lambda=0.25$ and $\Fish(\lambda)=1/\lambda^2$.
$\se(\hat\lambda)=\hat\lambda/\sqrt n=0.25/14.14=0.0177$.
If $\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta)\to\Normal(0,v)$ and $g$ is differentiable with $g'(\theta)\ne0$, then
\sqrt n\big(g(\hat\theta)-g(\theta)\big)\to\Normal\big(0,\ g'(\theta)^2v\big).
$g(\hat\theta)-g(\theta)=g'(\tilde\theta)(\hat\theta-\theta)$ for some $\tilde\theta$ between them. As $\tilde\theta\to\theta$, $g'(\tilde\theta)\to g'(\theta)$. Apply Slutsky.

The MLE of $\sigma$ in a normal sample is $\hat\sigma=\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2}$, where $\sqrt n(\hat\sigma^2-\sigma^2)\to\Normal(0,2\sigma^4)$. With $g(t)=\sqrt t$ we get $g'(\sigma^2)=1/(2\sigma)$. So $\sqrt n(\hat\sigma-\sigma)\to\Normal(0,\sigma^2/2)$ and $\se(\hat\sigma)\approx\sigma/\sqrt{2n}$.

A statistic $T=T(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ is sufficient for $\theta$ if the conditional distribution of the sample given $T$ does not depend on $\theta$. Once $T$ is known, the rest of the data carry no more information about $\theta$.
$T$ is sufficient for $\theta$ if and only if the joint density factors as
f(x_1,\dots,x_n;\theta)=g\big(T(\mathbf{x});\theta\big)\,h(\mathbf{x}),
where $h$ does not depend on $\theta$.
Bernoulli$(p)$: $f=p^{\sum x_i}(1-p)^{n-\sum x_i}$. So $T=\sum X_i$ (the number of successes).
Poisson$(\lambda)$: $f=e^{-n\lambda}\lambda^{\sum x_i}/\prod x_i!$. So $T=\sum X_i$.
Exponential$(\lambda)$: $f=\lambda^ne^{-\lambda\sum x_i}$. So $T=\sum X_i$.

$\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2)$: $\sum(x_i-\mu)^2=\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2+n(\bar{x}-\mu)^2$ shows $(\bar{X},S^2)$ is jointly sufficient for $(\mu,\sigma^2)$. For $\mu$ alone ($\sigma^2$ known), $\bar{X}$ is sufficient.
Uniform$(0,\theta)$: $f=\theta^{-n}\mathbf{1}\{\max x_i\le\theta\}$. So $T=\max X_i$.
By the factorisation, the likelihood depends on the data only through $T$. So the MLE is a function of any sufficient statistic. In every example above, the MLE is a function of $T$.

Let $\hat\Theta$ be an unbiased estimator of $\theta$ and $T$ a sufficient statistic. Then $\tilde\Theta=\Exp[\hat\Theta\mid T]$ is an estimator (sufficiency makes it free of $\theta$), it is unbiased, and
\Var(\tilde\Theta)\le\Var(\hat\Theta),
with equality only if $\hat\Theta$ is already a function of $T$.
Unbiased: $\Exp[\tilde\Theta]=\Exp\big[\Exp[\hat\Theta\mid T]\big]=\Exp[\hat\Theta]=\theta$.
By the law of total variance, $\Var[\hat\Theta]=\Var(\Exp[\hat\Theta\mid T])+\Exp[\Var(\hat\Theta\mid T)]\ge\Var[\tilde\Theta]$.

For a Bernoulli sample, $\hat\Theta=X_1$ is an unbiased (and very poor) estimator of $p$. With $T=\sum X_i$, $\Exp[X_1\mid T]=T/n=\bar{X}$, the sample proportion. Its variance $p(1-p)/n$ is far below $p(1-p)$. Conditioning on a sufficient statistic always helps.

A statistic $T$ is complete if $\Exp_\theta[\phi(T)]=0$ for all $\theta$ implies $\phi(T)=0$ with probability one. For one-parameter exponential families (normal with known variance, Bernoulli, Poisson, exponential), the natural sufficient statistic is complete.
If $T$ is complete and sufficient and $\phi(T)$ is an unbiased estimator of $\theta$, then $\phi(T)$ is the unique MVUE of $\theta$.

Take any unbiased estimator $\hat\Theta$. By Rao–Blackwell, $\Exp[\hat\Theta\mid T]$ is a function of $T$ with no larger variance. Two unbiased functions of $T$ differ by a function with zero mean, which is zero by completeness. So the Rao–Blackwellised estimator is unique, and it has minimum variance.

For $X_i\sim\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2)$, the MVUE of $\mu$ is $\bar{X}$ and the MVUE of $\sigma^2$ is $S^2$. Both are unbiased functions of the complete sufficient statistic $(\bar{X},S^2)$. This settles the questions of Chapter 1. For the uniform$(0,\theta)$ family, $\frac{n+1}n\max X_i$ is the MVUE of $\theta$.

A loss function $L(\hat\theta,\theta)$ is the cost of estimating $\theta$ by $\hat\theta$. Standard choices: squared error $(\hat\theta-\theta)^2$ and absolute error $\abs{\hat\theta-\theta}$. The Bayes risk of an estimator is the expected loss, averaged over the prior and the data.
With prior $\pi(\theta)$ and posterior $\pi(\theta\mid\mathbf{x})$, the estimator that minimises the Bayes risk is:
for squared-error loss, the posterior mean $\Exp[\theta\mid\mathbf{x}]$;
for absolute-error loss, the posterior median;
for $0$–$1$ loss, the posterior mode (MAP estimate).

Minimise $\Exp[(\theta-a)^2\mid\mathbf{x}]$ over $a$. Let $m=\Exp[\theta\mid\mathbf{x}]$ and write $(\theta-a)^2=(\theta-m)^2+2(\theta-m)(m-a)+(m-a)^2$. The cross term has zero posterior expectation. What remains is $\Var(\theta\mid\mathbf{x})+(m-a)^2$, minimised at $a=m$.
$X\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,p)$ with a $\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)$ prior gives the posterior $\mathrm{Beta}(a+x,b+n-x)$, with mean $\dfrac{a+x}{a+b+n}$ (Example 1.36). It is the weighted average
w\cdot\frac xn+(1-w)\cdot\frac a{a+b},\qquad w=\frac n{n+a+b}.
The Bayes estimator shrinks the MLE toward the prior mean. The prior acts like $a+b$ extra pseudo-observations.
As $n\to\infty$, $w\to1$, and the estimator approaches the MLE, with variance approaching the Cram'er–Rao bound.
For small $n$, shrinkage trades a little bias for a bigger drop in variance. This can lower the mean square error (compare Example 1.17).

blocks.name: Interview check
blocks.title: frequentist versus Bayesian in one paragraph

blocks.x: A frequentist treats $\theta$ as a fixed unknown and judges an estimator by its sampling distribution (bias, variance, coverage of intervals). A Bayesian treats $\theta$ as random with a prior, and reports the posterior.
A $95\%$ credible interval contains $\theta$ with posterior probability $0.95$. This is the statement people often wrongly read into a confidence interval.
For large samples with smooth priors the two approaches agree (Bernstein–von Mises: the posterior is approximately $\Normal(\hat\theta,1/(n\Fish(\hat\theta)))$). For small samples the prior matters.
Fisher information $\Fish(\theta)=\Var(\partial_\theta\ln f)=-\Exp[\partial_\theta^2\ln f]$ is the curvature of the log-likelihood. It adds up: $n\Fish$ for a sample of size $n$.
Cram'er–Rao: every unbiased estimator has $\Var\ge1/(n\Fish(\theta))$. $\bar{X}$ (normal mean), $\hat{P}$ (proportion) and $\bar{X}$ (Poisson and exponential mean) reach it.
The MLE is asymptotically $\Normal(\theta,1/(n\Fish))$: consistent, asymptotically unbiased and efficient. The delta method carries this to functions of $\theta$.

Sufficient statistics (factorisation theorem) keep all the information. Rao–Blackwell improves any unbiased estimator by conditioning on one. Lehmann–Scheff'e gives the unique MVUE from a complete sufficient statistic.
Bayes estimators are posterior summaries (the mean, for squared error). Conjugate priors give closed forms and shrinkage toward the prior mean.

Compute the Fisher information for (a) $\Normal(0,\sigma^2)$ with respect to $\sigma^2$, (b) the geometric distribution $f(x;p)=p(1-p)^{x-1}$, and give the Cram'er–Rao bound for unbiased estimators of $p$ based on a sample of size $n$.

Show that for a Poisson sample $\bar{X}$ attains the Cram'er–Rao bound for estimating $\lambda$, and that $\bar{X}^2-\bar{X}/n$ is an unbiased estimator of $\lambda^2$. Is it efficient for $\lambda^2$?
Prove the factorisation theorem in the discrete case (the easy direction: if the joint pmf factors as $g(T;\theta)h(\mathbf{x})$ then $T$ is sufficient).

Show that $\sum X_i$ is sufficient for $\lambda$ in a Poisson sample, and use Rao–Blackwell to improve the estimator $\mathbf{1}\{X_1=0\}$ of $e^{-\lambda}$; find its improved form $\big(\frac{n-1}n\big)^{T}$.
Using the delta method, find the approximate standard error of $\hat{p}/(1-\hat{p})$ (the odds) and of $\ln\big(\hat{p}/(1-\hat{p})\big)$ (the log-odds) for a binomial sample.

In a Bayesian analysis of $n=50$ trials with $x=7$ successes and a $\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)$ (uniform) prior, find the posterior mean, the posterior mode, and compare with the MLE and with a Wald interval.

For a $\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2)$ sample with known $\sigma^2$ and prior $\mu\sim\Normal(\mu_0,\tau^2)$, show that the Bayes estimator is $w\bar{x}+(1-w)\mu_0$ with $w=\dfrac{n/\sigma^2}{n/\sigma^2+1/\tau^2}$ and find its mean square error as a function of the true $\mu$. For which $\mu$ is it better than $\bar{X}$?
Prove that the MLE of $\theta$ in the uniform$(0,\theta)$ family is biased and find the bias; show that the bias-corrected estimator has variance $\theta^2/(n(n+2))$.
